column2: Why is it wrong to say that antibiotic exposure makes a bacterium generate the resistance mutation it needs?
column3: Mutations arise randomly during replication or repair and are then enriched by selection; the drug selects among existing variants rather than directing which mutation appears.

column2: How can resistance be selected even when plasma concentrations look adequate?
column3: Exposure differs across tissue, abscess, biofilm, gut, urine and intracellular compartments, and a subtherapeutic concentration at one of those sites can select resistant organisms.

column2: Why does reducing antimicrobial use not guarantee that population resistance falls quickly?
column3: Compensatory mutations lower the fitness cost without restoring susceptibility, and resistance can persist because its cost is low or because it is linked to other selected genes.

column2: What distinguishes transformation, transduction and conjugation?
column3: Transformation takes up naked environmental DNA, transduction moves bacterial genes inside bacteriophages, and conjugation transfers plasmids or other elements through direct cell contact.

column3: One plasmid may carry several resistance genes, so selecting for the plasmid with a single drug co-selects every resistance determinant it carries.

column2: What distinguishes tolerance, persistence and heteroresistance from inherited resistance?
column3: Tolerance is survival without a raised inhibitory concentration, persistence is a small phenotypic subpopulation surviving transient exposure, and heteroresistance is a resistant minority within an apparently susceptible isolate.

column2: Why is withholding necessary early therapy in severe infection not stewardship?
column3: Stewardship aims to keep treatment effective while reducing unnecessary selection, using narrow agents, optimised dosing, source control, timed review and shorter duration when evidence supports it.
